actual_prs.title: Exclude the query entity explicitly from LightFM similarity results
actual_prs.head: a85bcc5456aba5db8e3616a3b4c164bea7048f74
actual_prs.body:
### Description

LightFM's similarity helpers retrieve N + 1 candidates and discard the first result. When shared features produce tied cosine scores, that first result need not be the query: the query can remain in the returned recommendations while another eligible entity is omitted. Zero feature representations have the same problem.

Exclude the query by its ID before returning the first N sorted candidates. Apply the same small correction to both users and items, preserving cosine scores, descending order and the existing supported N range.

Fixes #2478.

### Validation

[Independent validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/recommenders/actions/runs/43918186395) checks exact head `a85bcc5456aba5db8e3616a3b4c164bea7048f74` with native LightFM 1.17:

| Python 3.11, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.13.1 | 4 passed, 1 skipped | 12 failed, 12 passed | 28 passed, 1 skipped |

The sole skip is the existing `test_fitting` marked as flaky upstream. All 24 new cases run. Local Python 3.12 gives the same results.

The tests train actual LightFM models and exercise shared, zero and distinct feature representations, every query ID, and N values 0, 1, 3 and 5. An independent float64 cosine calculation checks returned scores and top-N ordering without prescribing an arbitrary tie order. No model method is mocked.

Black and `git diff --check` pass. The validation workflow builds the unmodified official LightFM 1.17 revision with its Cython command; no dependency build changes are included in this PR.

### Description

`prepare_test_df` currently indexes the dictionary's key order to recover external IDs, ignoring the explicit internal indices stored in its values. Reconstructing an equivalent mapping in a different insertion order silently associates the same rating with a different user/item pair. NumPy conversion can also turn mixed integer/string IDs into strings.

Build the reverse lookups from the mapping values and apply them to the selected internal indices. Preserve external ID types and selected-row order, including repeated or Boolean selections. Fixes #2480.

actual_prs.title: Account for camera skew in pixel backprojection
actual_prs.head: e1bffa52bd561b37f7a6e786736ef6f11acf4a8e
actual_prs.body:
Closes #530.

`pixel2point` ignores the intrinsic matrix's skew entry, so it can return the wrong X coordinate after a valid `point2pixel` projection. The example in the issue reconstructs `[2.6, 3, 4]` instead of `[2, 3, 4]`. It also drops the derivative with respect to skew, even when evaluated at zero skew, which affects differentiable camera calibration.

Recover Y first and subtract the skew contribution before recovering X. The implementation keeps elementwise arithmetic, existing broadcasting and the zero-skew forward result.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- Four focused cases on unchanged main: **3 failed, 1 passed**.
- Patched complete repository suite: **404 passed, 18 skipped**. Skips require unavailable CUDA or the optional sparse backend.
- Positive/negative skew and a zero-skew control are compared with independently solved camera rays using batched intrinsics and shared depth; projection round-trips are checked.
- A separate gradient check compares skew, pixel and depth derivatives with the linear-solve reference. At zero skew, the original skew derivative is `0` instead of `-0.05` in this case.
- Additional native float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64 smoke checks recover the issue's original point exactly.
- `git diff --check` passes.

The existing camera-axis fix in #415 addresses a different cause. All 95 reachable historical geometry versions, including intermediate revisions and the earlier discussions, were checked; their four `pixel2point` variants all omit skew.

actual_prs.title: Keep similarity alignment temporaries on the input device
actual_prs.head: e06699f95d7781063b392792ea01dea010ffa281
actual_prs.body:
Closes #531.

`svdstf` constructs its determinant-correction matrix on the default device, while the SVD factors follow the explicit point-cloud inputs. This causes device mismatch during similarity alignment whenever these devices differ.

Pass `device=U.device` to the existing identity allocation. The SVD, determinant correction, scale calculation and Sim(3) result are otherwise unchanged.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- Focused cases on unchanged main: **2 failed, 2 passed, 2 skipped**. After the fix: **4 passed, 2 skipped**.
- CPU point clouds are aligned under both CPU and meta default-allocation contexts, with and without scale recovery. The actual point clouds, SVD and outputs remain CPU tensors. Results are checked against known rigid/similarity transforms.
- Optional native CUDA cases cover the ordinary CPU-default/CUDA-input combination; both skip because CUDA is unavailable here.
- Complete paired suites with seed 0: unchanged main **400 passed, 18 skipped**; patched **404 passed, 20 skipped**. The two additional skips are the explicit CUDA regressions.
- An initial unseeded patched run recorded **403 passed, 20 skipped and one failure** in the unchanged `TestOptim.test_optim_anybatch` convergence assertion. The paired seeded runs above pass that optimizer test; its code is untouched.
- `git diff --check` passes.

Reviewed all 95 reachable geometry source versions. The three historical `svdstf` implementations all omit the allocation device. #437 changes the separate `svdtf` reflection optimum and does not fix this allocation.

actual_prs.title: Reuse rotation matrices during IMU covariance propagation
actual_prs.head: 1f08d19c87272d10fc5b419cf79525e8d31604f5
actual_prs.body:
Closes #534.

Each covariance update converts the same `Rij` rotation to a matrix four times. Compute that matrix once and reuse it in the existing transition and acceleration-noise blocks. The temporary remains local to the call, with normal gradient tracking; no state is cached across updates.

## Measured effect

[Native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/actions/runs/43924450983) checks exact production head `1f08d19c87272d10fc5b419cf79525e8d31604f5` on PyTorch 2.5.1 and 2.6.0, Python 3.12, CPU.

Complete public `IMUPreintegrator.forward` calls, including integration, prediction and covariance propagation, were measured with synthetic IMU inputs. Each case uses four warmups and 21 alternating before/after pairs on one thread.

| Batch / frames | PyTorch 2.5.1 float32 before → after | Speedup across both versions and float32/float64 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 / 1 | 3.150 → 2.703 ms | 1.16–1.18× |
| 1 / 63 | 4.510 → 4.043 ms | 1.10–1.12× |
| 8 / 127 | 9.974 → 9.293 ms | 1.06–1.07× |
| 16 / 255 | 34.042 → 32.976 ms | 1.02–1.04× |

The gain is largest for short updates, where repeated conversions contribute more of the total work.

## Correctness

- Complete repository suite on both PyTorch versions: **400 passed, 18 skipped**. Skips require unavailable CUDA or the optional sparse backend.
- Every timed pair preserves all forward outputs bit for bit.
- Eighteen additional comparisons cover two dtypes, multiple batches, supplied/estimated rotations, stateful continuation with nonzero initial covariance, noise gradients, and direct covariance calls with rotation gradients.
- The benchmark imports the exact unchanged source from base commit `298e9f08` alongside the candidate. Its script and full results are retained in the linked validation run.
- `git diff --check` passes.

The change keeps the multiplication order and interval-noise expression intact, so it is separate from #451 and #507. All 77 reachable IMU source versions, including intermediate revisions and nine covariance-method variants, retain the repeated conversions.

actual_prs.title: Keep Cauchy costs finite when the input-to-scale ratio overflows
actual_prs.head: 4d265f813c0ff45834eb0cec60a4728f3c228472
actual_prs.body:
Closes #535.

`Cauchy` evaluates `x / delta**2` before taking the logarithm. That quotient can overflow even when both the input and the resulting robust cost are representable. For example, `delta=0.001` and float32 `x=1e34` currently produce an infinite cost and a zero derivative; the finite cost is approximately `9.21034e-5`.

Retain the direct expression while its quotient is safe. For larger ratios, evaluate the same logarithm using the inverse ratio and a difference of logarithms. Mask inputs before division so inactive branches cannot introduce invalid gradients. Half and bfloat16 intermediates use float32, and the result retains the floating input dtype. Integer promotion and gradients through a tensor-valued scale are preserved.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- Ten focused cases on unchanged main: **5 failed, 5 passed**.
- The ten new cases and ten existing Cauchy cases: **20 passed** after the fix.
- Complete repository suite with seed 0: **410 passed, 18 skipped**. Skips require unavailable CUDA or the optional sparse backend.
- Float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64 costs and input derivatives are checked against an independent 80-digit Decimal reference, including zero, the scale boundary and overflowing quotients.
- First- and second-order gradient checks cover the scale boundary; additional controls check integer-input promotion, tensor-scale gradients and subnormal-scale input gradients.
- A real Gauss–Newton update previously returned an infinite loss and left its parameter at `0.001`. It now returns a finite loss and reaches the expected `0.002` value.
- `git diff --check` passes.

#416 addresses cancellation near zero. This change addresses overflow for large input-to-scale quotients and retains the existing near-zero tests. All 24 reachable kernel source versions, including intermediate commits and three Cauchy implementations, still form the unbounded quotient.

actual_prs.title: Avoid computing discarded B-spline segment endpoints
actual_prs.body:
Closes #538.

`bspline` computes a right endpoint for every segment and then keeps only the final one. Select the final segment before the endpoint exponential and products. For N controls without extrapolation, the endpoint path now evaluates three Lie exponentials instead of 3*(N-3). The interior samples, cumulative spline formula and multiplication order are preserved.

## Measured effect

[Native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/actions/runs/43935472028) checks exact production head `f9f11dd001876446be1a1dc51477ec20e4e59743` on PyTorch 2.5.1 and 2.6.0, Python 3.12, CPU. It measures complete public interpolation calls with four warmups and 21 alternating before/after pairs on one thread. Inputs are synthetic SE3 trajectories.

| Batch / controls / interval | PyTorch 2.5.1 float32 before → after | PyTorch 2.6.0 float32 before → after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 / 64 / 0.1 | 4.813 → 4.688 ms | 4.752 → 4.584 ms |
| 1 / 1024 / 0.1 | 24.382 → 22.529 ms | 22.998 → 21.940 ms |
| 8 / 256 / 0.5 | 13.531 → 11.429 ms | 13.269 → 11.084 ms |
| 1 / 4096 / 0.5 | 24.472 → 19.868 ms | 23.766 → 19.137 ms |

Across all 28 timed cases, including float64 and both intervals, the observed speedup is 1.03–1.31×. The linked run retains every sample and the exact unchanged reference source is loaded from base commit `298e9f08`.

## Correctness

- Complete repository suite on both PyTorch versions: **422 passed, 18 skipped**. The skips require CUDA or the optional sparse backend.
- **24 focused tests passed on both unchanged and modified code**, including the existing spline tests. New controls check the independent cubic endpoint formula for commuting poses, short extrapolated trajectories, strided inputs and endpoint gradient locality.
- **60 complete-output/input-gradient comparisons per PyTorch version** cover float32/float64, three batch shapes, one/two/four/nine controls, extrapolation and strided inputs. All output values and input gradients are bitwise equal.
- Every timed call also checks all output poses for bitwise equality.
- `git diff --check` passes.

The history audit covers all 46 reachable spline commits and 31 source versions, including intermediate revisions. The adjacent-logarithm reuse in #497 leaves this endpoint computation intact. This patch changes only the work used to produce the final extra pose.

actual_prs.title: fix(sdk-python): release cancelled and failed control requests
actual_prs.body:
## What this PR does

Release a Python SDK control request's pending reply and timeout whenever the caller exits, including cancellation, write failure and drain failure. A reply or timeout that arrives during a failing write is consumed without replacing the caller's original error. Other requests keep their own replies and timers.

## Why it's needed

Cancelling a control request currently leaves its pending entry and timeout alive until another event happens to remove them. Repeated cancellation therefore retains work that has no caller, and a delayed failure can produce an unhandled future exception. A failed write has the same ownership problem.

## Reviewer Test Plan

### How to verify

1. Cancel several control requests after the peer receives them. Their pending entries and timeout callbacks should disappear immediately, while a separate request should still receive its own response.
2. Fail a write, fail a drain, or cancel while a drain is blocked. The caller should retain the original failure or cancellation, with no abandoned request state.
3. Allow a request to time out while its drain is blocked, then fail that drain. The original drain error should be preserved and the event loop should not report an unhandled future exception.

### Evidence (Before & After)

The five new regression cases fail on the unchanged base and pass with this change. The complete local Python SDK suite reports **192 passed, 26 skipped**. Python linting and the configured type check pass. An independent rerun of the original reproduction reports **2 passed**: all 16 cancelled requests leave zero retained entries and zero live timeout callbacks, failed writes leave no event-loop warning, and a later independent request succeeds.

[Official upstream CI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948450440/job/133584322380) now passes the selected Linux workspace build and static checks. [Python SDK checks](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948450628/job/133584302154) pass on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12. Both selected Linux unit-test shards also pass. The earlier local build attempts ended during CLI TypeScript compilation with status 137. The complete preflight and official CLI end-to-end coverage remain unverified, so this PR stays Draft; a successful selected CI job is not evidence that the skipped integration jobs ran.

### Tested on

| OS | Status |
| --- | --- |
| 🍏 macOS | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🪟 Windows | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🐧 Linux | ✅ Local Python SDK tests; official Linux build/static checks and Python 3.10–3.12 checks |

### Environment (optional)

Python 3.12.14 on Linux. Node.js 24.22.1 and the pinned pnpm 11.24.0 were used for the attempted workspace build.

## Risk & Scope

- Main risk or tradeoff: cleanup must remain idempotent when cancellation, a reply, timeout or shutdown coincide. The regression cases cover those competing outcomes without changing the original exception seen by the caller.
- Not validated / out of scope: a permanently blocked drain, official CLI end-to-end behavior, macOS, Windows and the complete repository preflight.
- Breaking changes / migration notes: no public API or protocol change.

## Linked Issues

Fixes #17494.

<details>
<summary>中文说明</summary>

## 本次修改

无论调用者正常结束、取消请求、写入失败还是等待写出失败，都释放 Python SDK 控制请求所持有的待回复状态和超时任务。如果写入尚未完成时已经收到回复或触发超时，会处理相应的完成状态，同时保留调用者原本应收到的异常。其他请求仍使用各自独立的回复和计时器。

## 修改原因

目前取消控制请求后，其待回复记录和超时任务会一直保留，直到其他事件恰好清除它们。反复取消因此会留下已没有调用者等待的工作，随后发生的失败还可能引发未处理的 future 异常。写入失败也存在相同的资源归属问题。

## 审查者验证计划

### 验证方式

1. 在对端收到请求后取消多条控制请求。对应的待回复记录和超时回调应立即消失，另一条独立请求仍应收到自己的回复。
2. 分别触发写入失败、等待写出失败，以及等待写出受阻时的取消。调用者应保留原始异常或取消结果，不留下无人使用的请求状态。
3. 在等待写出受阻期间让请求超时，然后令等待写出失败。调用者应收到原始写出异常，事件循环不应报告未处理的 future 异常。

### 修改前后证据

新增的五个回归用例在未修改基线上失败，修改后通过。完整的本地 Python SDK 测试结果为 **192 通过、26 跳过**，Python lint 和配置的类型检查均通过。独立重新运行原始复现脚本的结果为 **2 通过**：16 条取消请求均未残留待回复记录或活动计时器，写入失败没有产生事件循环警告，之后的独立请求可以成功完成。

[上游官方 CI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948450440/job/133584322380) 已通过选定的 Linux 工作区构建和静态检查；[Python SDK 检查](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948450628/job/133584302154) 在 Python 3.10、3.11 和 3.12 上均通过。选定的两个 Linux 单元测试分片也均已通过。此前本地构建尝试在 CLI 的 TypeScript 编译阶段以状态码 137 结束。完整 preflight 和官方 CLI 端到端覆盖仍未建立，因此本 PR 保持 Draft；选定 CI 检查通过不能证明已跳过的集成测试执行过。

### 测试平台

| 系统 | 状态 |
| --- | --- |
| 🍏 macOS | ⚠️ 未测试 |
| 🪟 Windows | ⚠️ 未测试 |

actual_prs.body:
## What this PR does

Wait for an in-flight Python SDK process startup before closing the query, then shut down the resulting process and its background work. Repeated shutdown remains harmless, including shutdown requested from an input generator's cleanup.

## Why it's needed

Closing a query while process creation is suspended can currently return before that process exists. Startup can then finish after the query has been marked closed, leaving a live child behind. This matters when applications cancel startup or leave a query context quickly.

## Reviewer Test Plan

### How to verify

1. Pause process creation, begin closing the query, and then allow creation to finish. Shutdown should wait and should return only after the child has exited.
2. Request shutdown twice during the same pending startup. Both callers should finish without leaving a child or background work alive.
3. Close before startup, and repeat shutdown after completion. Both operations should remain safe.
4. Let an asynchronous input generator request shutdown from its cleanup. Cleanup should finish without waiting on itself.

### Evidence (Before & After)

The original local reproduction starts a real Python child. On the unchanged base that child remains alive after shutdown returns; with this change it has exited when shutdown finishes. The new regression cases cover pending startup, concurrent shutdown callers, shutdown before startup and reentrant generator cleanup. The complete local Python SDK suite reports **192 passed, 26 skipped**. Python linting and the configured type check pass. An independent rerun of the original reproduction together with existing single-query and asynchronous-context happy paths reports **3 passed**.

[Official upstream CI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948503619/job/133584543040) now passes the selected Linux workspace build and static checks. [Python SDK checks](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43948503307/job/133584492088) pass on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12. Both selected Linux unit-test shards also pass. The earlier local build attempts ended during CLI TypeScript compilation with status 137. The complete preflight and official CLI end-to-end coverage remain unverified, so this PR stays Draft; a successful selected CI job is not evidence that the skipped integration jobs ran.

### Tested on

| OS | Status |
| --- | --- |
| 🍏 macOS | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🪟 Windows | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🐧 Linux | ✅ Local Python SDK tests; official Linux build/static checks and Python 3.10–3.12 checks |

### Environment (optional)

Python 3.12.14 on Linux. Node.js 24.22.1 and the pinned pnpm 11.24.0 were used for the attempted workspace build.

## Risk & Scope

- Main risk or tradeoff: shutdown now waits for process creation that is already in progress. The existing early-closed guard is preserved so an input generator can finish its own cleanup without a reentrant deadlock.
- Not validated / out of scope: indefinitely stalled process creation, cancellation of shutdown itself, official CLI end-to-end behavior, macOS, Windows and the complete repository preflight.
- Breaking changes / migration notes: no public API or protocol change; shutdown now waits for the resource it is responsible for releasing.

## Linked Issues

Fixes #17493.

actual_prs.body:
## What this PR does

Keep the Python SDK's shared initialization alive when one waiting control call is cancelled. Other waiting calls, later calls and prompt input can continue after the initialization reply. Query-owned shutdown still stops those continuations before they write another prompt or control request.

## Why it's needed

Every initialization waiter currently awaits the same task directly. Cancelling one public call therefore cancels the shared handshake, an unrelated waiting call and prompt input. The transport remains open, but the query can no longer make useful progress. Isolating caller cancellation also requires checking whether the query closed during the handshake, so an initialization error cannot let waiting work resume after shutdown.

## Reviewer Test Plan

### How to verify

1. Delay the initialization reply, start two independent control calls and cancel only one. Deliver a successful initialization reply. The cancelled call should report cancellation, the other call and a later call should receive their own responses, and the prompt should be sent once.
2. Repeat with both a string prompt and asynchronous input. Include an uncancelled control to verify normal startup behavior.
3. Close the query during initialization, then separately reject initialization. Waiting controls must terminate and neither input form may write after shutdown. Background input must not produce an unhandled exception.

### Evidence (Before & After)

The eight new regression cases report **4 failed, 4 passed** on the unchanged base and **8 passed** with this change. The complete local Python SDK suite reports **195 passed, 26 skipped**, with Python linting and the configured type check passing. An independent rerun of the original four-case reproduction reports **4 passed** against the exact proposed commit: cancellation stays with the selected caller, unrelated and later calls succeed, each input form writes one prompt, and the input task is not cancelled.

[Official upstream CI](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43955496117/job/133608965234) now passes the selected Linux workspace build and static checks. [Python SDK checks](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/actions/runs/43955496170/job/133608908711) pass on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12. Both selected Linux unit-test shards now pass. The latest check snapshot contains 20 successful checks and 26 skipped checks, with none still running. The earlier local build attempts ended during CLI TypeScript compilation with status 137. The complete preflight and official CLI end-to-end coverage remain unverified, so this PR stays Draft; a successful selected CI job is not evidence that the skipped integration jobs ran.

### Tested on

| OS | Status |
| --- | --- |
| 🍏 macOS | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🪟 Windows | ⚠️ Not tested |
| 🐧 Linux | ✅ Local Python SDK tests; official Linux build/static checks and Python 3.10–3.12 checks |

### Environment (optional)

Python 3.12.14 on Linux. Node.js 24.22.1 and the pinned pnpm 11.24.0 were used for the attempted workspace build.

## Risk & Scope

- Main risk or tradeoff: isolating cancellation must preserve query-owned shutdown and initialization failure. The regression cases check both outcomes and require that no prompt or control is written after shutdown.
- Not validated / out of scope: official CLI end-to-end behavior, macOS, Windows and the complete repository preflight.
- Breaking changes / migration notes: no public API or protocol change. Cancelling one waiting call no longer cancels unrelated calls or input.

## Linked Issues

Fixes #17496.

actual_prs.title: perf(lqr): avoid retaining unused control increments
actual_prs.body:
## Motivation and change

Closes #540.

The LQR rollout allocates a complete control-increment trajectory, writes one slice, reads that slice immediately, and never uses it again. Keep the current increment in a local tensor before adding the nominal control. The feedback law, returned state/control trajectories, cost accumulation and public interface stay the same.

This removes one control-sized history allocation and one chain of indexed autograd writes. For a batch of 64, horizon 256, four controls and float64, the omitted history alone is 524,288 bytes. That is an allocation-size statement, not a claim about overall peak memory.

## Correctness

The new tests solve the complete finite-horizon quadratic problem independently as one condensed dense system, rather than repeating the Riccati recursion. Sixteen cases cover float32/float64, zero/nonzero nominal controls, batch sizes 1/3 and horizons 1/8. They compare all returned trajectories and costs, plus a weighted-square output functional's gradients with respect to the initial state and linear cost.

[Native validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/actions/runs/43960623977) on the exact proposed source:

- PyTorch 2.5.1 and 2.6.0: the new 16-case oracle passes on the unchanged source; the complete candidate suite reports **416 passed, 18 skipped** on each version.
- An additional 16-case unchanged/candidate comparison has exactly equal outputs, and exactly equal initial-state/linear-cost gradients in its eight training cases.
- A separate source review found no blocking algorithm or oracle issue. Higher-order gradients and gradients of every system parameter are not claimed by these checks.

## Measured effect

CPU, one thread, PyTorch 2.6.0, nonzero warm starts. Each implementation gets twelve permuted measurements after warm-up, with two identical unchanged implementations to show timing noise. These are complete controller calls plus backward, not an isolated tensor operation.

| Batch / horizon / state / control / dtype | Unchanged A (ms) | Unchanged B (ms) | Proposed (ms) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 / 32 / 4 / 2 / float64 | 25.068 | 24.928 | 23.980 |
| 16 / 128 / 4 / 2 / float32 | 112.438 | 112.087 | 108.596 |
| 64 / 256 / 8 / 4 / float64 | 569.474 | 563.592 | 539.041 |

The observed training medians are 3.1–5.3% lower than the two controls across these cases. Forward-only measurements are also included in the raw results; they show a smaller effect. This is CPU evidence for these shapes, not a GPU or universal throughput claim.

For the largest case, the graph has **1,024 rather than 1,280 CopySlices nodes**. The profiler's sum of positive per-event self CPU allocation accounting decreases from **2,814,210,315 to 2,519,582,723 bytes** (about 10.5%). This cumulative accounting includes repeated allocations during forward/backward; it is not process peak memory.

[Full measurements and exact samples](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/blob/7aee6a2a3cdaf54c9e2f734d37588414bf334453/.audit/lqr-increment-storage/results.json) · [validation summary](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/blob/7aee6a2a3cdaf54c9e2f734d37588414bf334453/.audit/lqr-increment-storage/validation-summary.json)

## Scope and prior work

This is independent of the earlier triangular-solver proposal and module-conversion fixes. The history audit includes upstream PR refs and the fork's branches and intermediate commits: 115 prior source blobs and 44 distinct rollout variants. The nominal-increment variants retain a complete tensor or list; the older direct-linear rollouts do not implement the nominal-increment algorithm. No equivalent removal was found. [History evidence](https://github.com/Afloat16/pypose/blob/7aee6a2a3cdaf54c9e2f734d37588414bf334453/.audit/lqr-increment-storage/history-summary.json).

Only the rollout change and its independent regression tests are in the proposed branch. Validation workflows, benchmarks and logs remain in the separate evidence branch.
